1292917512/AnelfAgent.description: Implements a fully personal terminal based on an agent.
1292917512/AnelfAgent.body:
# AnelfAgent

**v0.3** · Unified agent framework — autonomous thinking · semantic memory · tool orchestration · multimodal generation · real-time voice · multi-channel communication

**Simplified Chinese** | [English](https://github.com/1292917512/AnelfAgent/blob/HEAD/README_EN.md)

AnelfAgent is an open-source, self-hosted AI agent runtime. Give it an LLM API key and it becomes an AI assistant that **has its own memory, learns skills on its own, takes initiative to get work done, and lives across multiple chat platforms**. It includes an autonomous decision engine, hybrid semantic memory, skill self-learning, sub-agent scheduling, resumable workflows, MCP tool bridging, and multi-platform channel adapters. It covers multimodal capabilities for text, images, voice, video, and music, and ships with a modern WebUI for all configuration, conversation, and operations.

> This repository is the **0.3 stable baseline**: the architecture and capabilities have largely settled, and it is suited to self-hosted deployment and further extension.

---

## Quick Start

> Goal: **get the agent running within 5 minutes**. You only need Python, Node.js, and an LLM API key.

### 1. Requirements

| Dependency | Version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python | **3.11 ~ 3.12** | Main runtime |
| Node.js | **24** (recommended, see `.nvmrc`; minimum 22.12) | Builds the WebUI frontend; the agent still runs without building it (just no web interface) |
| [uv](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) | Latest | Python package manager (strongly recommended; the startup script uses it to install dependencies automatically) |

### 2. Clone and Configure

```bash
git clone https://github.com/1292917512/AnelfAgent.git
cd AnelfAgent

# Create the three core config files from templates
cp config/llm_clients.example.json config/llm_clients.json
cp config/app_config.example.json config/app_config.json
cp config/mcp_servers.example.json config/mcp_servers.json
```

Next, open `config/llm_clients.json` and enter your key in the `api_key` field of any one provider (OpenAI / Anthropic / DeepSeek / Zhipu and 100+ other providers are all supported, unified through litellm). **To start, you only need one working chat model and one embedding model; everything else can be configured in the WebUI…**

The repository bound to the task board requires write access: creating new labels requires push permission, and labeling issues requires triage or higher. With read-only access, you can create and read issues, but adding labels, label transitions, and wayfinder labels are unavailable.

```bash
# ① Install the DSH CLI (skip if already installed)
npm install -g @deepseek-ai/dsh

# ② Install MattSkillsDeck — --profile is required: install it into the profile that matches the DSH entry point you actually use

#     or
dsh plugin --profile desktop add dsh-mattpocock-skills-deck   # for the DSH Desktop app

dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-mattpocock-skills-deck@1.7.51 --registry https://registry.npmjs.org
#     or
dsh plugin --profile desktop add dsh-mattpocock-skills-deck@1.7.51 --registry https://registry.npmjs.org
```

# OpenCode Buddy

A VS Code extension that brings the **opencode** agent into a full chat GUI. The original motivation was that the existing VS Code opencode plugin was too difficult to use, and the cc-gui open source project was found on GitHub. It is a greenfield port of the IntelliJ plugin [`jetbrains-cc-gui`](https://github.com/zhukunpenglinyutong/jetbrains-cc-gui): the React webview is carried over verbatim, the Java backend is rewritten in TypeScript, and only the **opencode** provider is kept (Claude / Codex / Grok / Kimi / PI branches removed).

Unlike the original plugin — which spawned a fresh `opencode run` process for every message — this extension keeps a **persistent `opencode serve` daemon** (via `@opencode-ai/sdk`) alive across all tabs and conversations, managed by a daemon bridge with prewarm, heartbeat, crash-restart, and session reuse.

## Philosophy

[`jetbrains-cc-gui`](https://github.com/zhukunpenglinyutong/jetbrains-cc-gui) aims to provide a unified experience across different AI providers. This project takes a different approach — it **reuses opencode's capabilities without secondary development**, focusing on providing a native GUI experience for…

# Daily Agent Benchmarks

**Live site: https://xbsleepy.github.io/daily-agent-benchmarks/** · [Archive](https://xbsleepy.github.io/daily-agent-benchmarks/archive.html) · [Atom feed](https://xbsleepy.github.io/daily-agent-benchmarks/feed.xml)

A daily, searchable list of new **AI / LLM agent benchmarks** on arXiv — web agents, GUI & computer-use agents, coding / SWE agents, tool use, multi-agent, embodied, and agent safety evaluations. Each paper gets a page with authors, abstract, field, citation count, and arXiv PDF / HTML links. Updated automatically every day via GitHub Actions.

Collects Agent Benchmark papers from [arXiv](https://arxiv.org) daily and organizes them into a static site that can be deployed to GitHub Pages.

The site displays entries in reverse chronological order of submission date: name, authors, abstract, categories, and PDF / HTML links. Each day has a bilingual Chinese-English briefing. In-browser ranked search uses **BM25**.

## What this repository does

1. **Runs once a day** (GitHub Actions, or manually run locally) and calls the arXiv API.
2. **Keeps only Agent Benchmarks**: first recalls papers with agent + benchmark related queries, then filters them with keyword scoring (LLM agent, web/GUI/coding agent, tool-use, computer-use, etc.). It excludes ordinary RL agents, reagents / pathogens, and other unrelated uses.
3. **Merges into the index** `docs/data/index.json`, grouped by the `published` date.
4. **Generates the daily briefing** (no paid model required): topic statistics plus the first sentence of the abstracts of high-scoring papers, one each in Chinese and English.
5. **GitHub Pages** reads this JSON to render the page. Search runs in the browser and does not depend on a backend.

brycewang-stanford/StatsPAI.description: StatsPAI is the first Agent-native Python library for causal inference and applied econometrics — unified API, broad cross-method coverage, structured result objects, machine-readable schemas, Skills, an MCP server, and R/Stata parity validation.
brycewang-stanford/StatsPAI.body: Simplified Chinese (default) | [English](https://github.com/brycewang-stanford/statspai/blob/main/README_EN.md) # StatsPAI: A Stata/R Alternative Designed for Agents      Developed and maintained by the Stanford REAP team Paper published in the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS): Wang & Rozelle (2026), 11(125), 10604 · doi:10.21105/joss.10604 StatsPAI is for empirical researchers who previously had to switch back and forth between Stata, R, and Python. Its goal is straightforward: bring common econometrics, causal inference, diagnostics, robustness checks, table export, and agent-readable metadata into a single Python-native API. You can think of it as a drop-in Stata/R alternative entry point for new projects: - Stata-style: `regress`, `ivregress`, `reghdfe`, `csdid`, `rdrobust`, `synth`, `psmatch2`, `esttab` / `outreg2`. - R-style: `lm`, `fixest`, `did`, `rdrobust`, `Synth`, `DoubleML`, `MatchIt`, `modelsummary`, `broom`. - Key behaviors follow Stata conventions: `regress`, `ivreg`, and the various likelihood-based estimators all accept `vce="robust"` / `vce="cluster firm"`; robust and clustered standard errors use Stata's small-sample corrections and z / t reference distributions; after any fitted result you can run `test` / `lincom` / `margins, dydx()`; existing Stata command lines can run directly via `sp.stata("...", data=df)`. - Python output: on supported result objects, call `.summary()`, `.tidy()`, `.plot()`, `.to_latex()`, `.to_docx()`, or `.to_agent_summary()` directly. - Agent-native: every public function ships with a machine-readable schema in the registry (`sp.list_functions()`, `sp.describe_function()`, `sp.function_schema()`), and the bundled `statspai-mcp`…

cubxxw/blog.body:
· 
   · 

## This Is Not a Knowledge Repository

Knowledge is becoming infinite, instant, and increasingly cheap. Organizing one more set of concepts or restating one more consensus has limited value.

What is truly scarce is what remains after knowledge passes through a specific person, a real experience, and actual work: what was done, why it was done that way, where it failed, and how judgment changed as a result.

> AI can rewrite a passage of text, but it cannot experience a failure for me, make a choice for me, or pay the price of a long-term judgment for me.
>
> This repository stores exactly those parts that cannot be ghostwritten.

[cubxxw.com](https://cubxxw.com/zh/) is my public writing workshop. There are no “learn a new concept every day” tasks here, and no chasing answers that merely look correct. Articles only settle three kinds of things: practices I have personally verified, reusable workflows, and reflections that hold up when looked back on.

## Three Lines I Will Keep Writing

**01 / Turning AI into a system that truly works**

Not just discussing models and prompts, but studying how Agents, context, memory, evaluation, safety boundaries, and automation enter real production workflows. This keeps the architectural choices, and also keeps the scene of the failures.

**02 / Turning information into a personal capability**

Information is not knowledge, and collecting is not owning. I continually break down my own knowledge management, second brain, content creation, and personal workflows, caring about how they move through “information → recording → knowledge → creation” and finally reach action.

**03 / Continuing to be a concrete person as machines grow stronger**

Beyond technology, I write about choices, relationships, identity, risk, cities, and travel. Not to summarize life into rules, but to leave honest enough field evidence: where I am, what I have gone through, and how I have been changed by it.

Technical articles will try to give reproducible paths, reflective articles will explain their reasoning, and personal articles will preserve the scene. Together they answer the same question:

> As more and more abilities can be outsourced to AI, what must still be done by oneself?

## Start Here

If this is your first time here, these articles come closest to the core of this repository:

- [One person leading a team of Agents to reassemble a blog of 120+ articles](https://cubxxw.com/zh/ai-agent/posts/ai-native-blog-rebuild/) — a real large-scale Agent collaboration, not an automation fantasy.

kunpeng9/GTD2020-05-31.body:
Some things got mixed together before, and I deleted them haphazardly. The file extension should be changed to html.

I'll look at the content of your issues page first.
Then I'll sample the topic distribution of your early issues, and also look up cutting-edge global change log and document management practices for reference.
That's enough information. Now I'll turn the plan into ready-to-use files: a directory template, an automatic export script, and a GitHub Actions workflow.
I've reviewed your latest 10 issues (#1730–#1739), your earliest 10 (#1–#10), and a mid-range sample (#393–#402). First the conclusions, then the plan.

## 1. Diagnosis: Three major problems with using issues as a knowledge base

The records show three problems directly:

1. **No categorization.** Among the 1,700+ entries, AI chat archives, software complaints, sci-fi setting analysis, professional research, and social issues are all mixed together. You yourself complained about this in #1739;
2. **Formatting loss.** As you said in #1730, “tables stored in knowledge management software get lost and turn into a jumbled mess.” The same problem exists in GitHub issues (titles render blank), whereas Markdown files in a repository render tables natively;
3. **The real pain point isn't “where to record,” but commit friction.** In #1739 you wrote: “Every time before committing I have to fill in the change log. It would be easier to just record it in the issue and click to commit.”

Point 3 is exactly the problem that cutting-edge global engineering practices are designed to solve, and the plan below is built around it.

## 2. Directory structure: six-category docs layout

Based on the actual content distribution of your issues (topics shown by the sample), I recommend a fixed set of 6 categories, numbered and sorted, without bloat:

```
├── README.md        ← Landing page + navigation

│   └── journal/                    ← Diary stream, one file per month, e.g. 2026-09.md

```

# Qingliao 3.0 (轻聊) — Native iOS AI Assistant

An AI assistant client for home NAS, native SwiftUI (not an HTML wrapper), connecting to a self-hosted backend (Hermes + custom Python service). It provides AI chat, a smart home dashboard (Home Assistant), NAS/router status, Docker management, a knowledge base, AI memory, password management, scheduled tasks, and more. Requires iOS 17+ (tested on iOS 26/27), distributed via SideStore sideloading.

> 🔗 **Backend is open source**: The backend service paired with this app (unified API, Docker deployment) is open-sourced at [`github.com/lxm20060513-svg/qingliao-backend`](https://github.com/lxm20060513-svg/qingliao-backend) (MIT). It includes `docker-compose` + `.env.example` + full deployment docs. For deployment or upgrades, refer to that repository.

> This document is for **AI agents taking over development and releases**: after reading it, you can independently complete the full flow of "change feature → self-check → release → deliver".
>
> Note: internal handoff and operations docs (release history, ops manual, internal health-check records) are **not included in this public repo** and remain only in the deployment environment.

---

## 🚀 Quick Start (Development Environment)

- Default branch: **`feature/handoff-301`** (the current 3.x development and release line, and the default branch on GitHub). `native-3.0` is the early 3.0 mainline; it is hundreds of commits behind this branch and is no longer the default branch.
- **2.0 is concluded** (final version v2.0.140): history is frozen on branch `native-2.0` + tag `v2.0.140`. 2.0 artifacts are archived in NAS `轻聊app/archive/2.0-final/`. 3.0 was branched from the 2.0 HEAD, so git history is complete.
- The project is generated by **XcodeGen** (`project.yml`). The source directory `qingliao/` is globbed as a whole, so **new .swift files require no change to project.yml**.
- `check_swift.sh`: a **swiftc -parse pure syntax check** on Linux (whole project). **⚠️ It only checks syntax, not types, scope, or concurrency.** Type errors, methods inserted into the wrong struct, and @MainActor violations only surface during CI compilation. (v2.0.90 real-world incident: a method was mistakenly placed inside the PasswordSheet struct; syntax checks all passed, but CI reported `cannot find in scope`.)

```bash
./check_swift.sh        # run before committing (output must say "all passed")
```

> [!NOTE]
> This project is currently under development. It does not yet match modern browsers, but it works well enough to display basic web pages.

> [!TIP]
> Code documentation is available below. We always keep it up to date with the latest dev branch.
>
> https://orinium-browser.github.io/orinium/orinium_browser/

## Separating the Web from specific companies' implementations

Orinium is a browser engine that aims to return the Web to an open runtime environment that does not depend on the implementations or policies of any particular company, and that users and developers can control.

Currently, many browsers depend on Chromium. Chromium is an excellent open-source project, but when a single implementation becomes the de facto standard for the entire Web, it affects the diversity and independence of the Web.

When browser engines concentrate in a single direction, the interpretation of Web standards, the spread of non-standard features, and future technical choices may be largely determined by the judgment of one organization.

Orinium is not a project to eliminate Google. It aims to avoid creating points of control by any specific company, and to remain an open technical foundation where anyone can participate in and improve the Web.

## Extension formats

In the future, this browser engine will support extensions. The formats currently planned for support are:

- Orinium's own format
- Firefox addons
- Chromium manifest v2 (partial)

Supporting these will help maintain compatibility with other browsers, and Orinium's own features suited to this browser can provide a better user experience.

## Run

Clone the repository.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/orinium-browser/orinium.git
cd orinium
```

You can run it using Cargo.

```bash
cargo run
```

> [!NOTE]
> It has been confirmed that installing the following packages on Ubuntu may be necessary.
>
> ```bash
> sudo apt install pkg-config libasound2-dev
> ```

### Development tests

# Show the list of commands
cargo run --example tests help

vhukze/DataDjinn.body:
---

## Introduction

DataDjinn is a local database client for Windows. It combines connection management, object browsing, SQL editing, data editing, import/export, and optional AI, MCP, Git sync, and version management capabilities in one desktop workspace. Core features work out of the box, while larger or more dependency-heavy capabilities are installed on demand.

Current latest version: `v0.3.20`

## Core Capabilities

- Multi-database connections: SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, DM (Dameng), GaussDB, MongoDB, Redis, ClickHouse, Elasticsearch.
- Connection tree: groups and subgroups, drag-and-drop sorting, pinning, search and locate, SSH tunnels, connection testing, reconnecting after saving a password, silent reconnection, and multiple connection import/export formats. Group, sort, and database display preferences are kept across restarts and updates. Opening a connection expands only the connection level; databases, schemas, and table groups are expanded manually as needed. Background table size statistics preserve expanded fields and click position.
- SQL workspace: Monaco editor, multi-tab queries, SQL and stored procedure completion, keyword highlighting, statement-level execution, and per-statement result display. Supports completing fields by typing a field name prefix or a table alias followed by a dot, and is compatible with DM table name case sensitivity.
- Data browsing and editing: WHERE filtering, pagination, column search, column width and order adjustment, Excel-style Ctrl/Shift multi-select, row and column selection, batch editing, draft state, and submission. Double-clicking a table immediately opens the work page with a single loading icon, and no blank row-number grid is shown during the first read.
- Table structure and objects: browse databases, schemas, tables, views, stored procedures, collections, and Redis keys; view DDL, and create and modify relational table structures.
- Data migration: batched import/export of SQL, CSV, JSON, and Markdown; relational database backup and restore; MongoDB and Redis JSON export. Redis full-database export includes all keys.
- Security and experience: Windows DPAPI local password protection, light/dark themes, custom title bar, and background update detection. Only officially released main program versions are recognized, and failed background checks never interrupt operations with a dialog. Installed versions update automatically through the standard installer and reopen; the update entry no longer launches a command-line window.
